group.passage: Next time you visit a temple in Taiwan, look up at the roof. You may see dragons, phoenixes, birds, and flowers shining in bright colors on top of it. Many of these figures are made with an art called jiannian, a Chinese name that means “cut and paste.” On the roofs of Longshan Temple in Taipei, for example, dragons and phoenixes are covered with colorful pieces of glass and ceramics, while other figures on temple roofs show characters from well-known folk stories. Making one of these figures takes three main steps. First, the artists bend steel wire into a frame, which works a bit like a skeleton. Next, they cover the frame with a paste made from sticky rice and lime, and this paste gives the figure its body. Finally, they break or cut ceramic bowls into small pieces, shape them, and press them into the paste. When the work is done well, the colors can stay bright for more than 30 years, but cheaper methods fall apart much more quickly. The art did not begin in Taiwan. It started around 1600 in Chaozhou, a city in China's Guangdong Province. Chaozhou was a busy center for making ceramics, so there was plenty of broken pottery for artists to use. Later, immigrants brought the art to Taiwan, where it grew into a local style with Taoist themes and wishes for good luck. Today, however, the art faces a serious problem. The job is no picnic: the artists work long hours high up on roofs in very hot and very cold weather, and breaking pottery can cut their hands. It also takes years of patient practice to learn the skills. In 2004, a survey found only 37 registered jiannian artists in Taiwan. As these masters grow older, passing on their skills has become a real challenge. In 2026, a training center opened in Pingtung to teach new workers this art and other skills that are needed to repair old buildings.

translation_zh.text:
下次你到台灣的廟宇參觀時，抬頭看看屋頂。你可能會看到龍、鳳、鳥和花在屋頂上閃耀著鮮豔的色彩。這些造型很多是用一種叫做「剪黏」的藝術做成的，這個中文名稱的意思是「剪下再黏上」。例如台北龍山寺的屋頂上，龍和鳳都覆蓋著五顏六色的玻璃和陶瓷碎片；廟宇屋頂上的其他造型則呈現大家熟悉的民間故事人物。
做一件這樣的作品主要有三個步驟。首先，匠師把鋼絲彎成骨架，作用有點像骨骼。接著，他們用糯米和石灰做成的黏料把骨架包起來，這層黏料塑出了作品的形體。最後，他們把陶瓷碗敲碎或剪成小片，修整形狀後壓進黏料裡。做得好的作品，顏色可以鮮豔超過 30 年；較便宜的做法則壞得快得多。
這門藝術並不是從台灣開始的。它大約在 1600 年起源於中國廣東省的潮州。潮州是製作陶瓷的重鎮，所以有大量的破碎陶器可以讓匠師使用。後來，移民把這門藝術帶到台灣，在這裡發展出帶有道教主題與祈求好運的在地風格。
然而，這門藝術如今面臨一個嚴重的問題。這份工作一點也不輕鬆：匠師要在很熱和很冷的天氣裡，長時間在高高的屋頂上工作，而敲碎陶器可能割傷他們的手。要學會這些技術也需要多年耐心的練習。2004 年的一項調查發現，台灣登記在案的剪黏匠師只有 37 位。隨著這些師傅年紀漸長，傳承他們的技藝成了真正的挑戰。2026 年，屏東開設了一個培訓中心，教導新的工作者這門藝術以及修復老建築所需的其他技藝。
